newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African gold shares spooked as metal hits $350.
newsitem.headline: S.African gold shares spooked as metal hits $350.

text.p: South African gold shares took a further pounding on Wednesday as the gold price fell below the psychologically-important $350 per ounce to its lowest level in 3-1/4 years.
The Johannesburg Stock Exchange's gold share index shed three percent by early afternoon to reach a new one-year low.
Dealers said the weak gold price augured ill for South African mines, especially because forecasts of a steadier rand in 1997 offer little hope of better gold prices in rand terms.
The latest jolt to the market comes in the middle of South African mines' reporting season for the quarter which ended in December.
Results from those companies which have so far reported -- Gold Fields of South Africa Ltd, Gencor Ltd and JCI Ltd -- have been encouraging. But this has been overshadowed by the bullion price.
"The gold quarterly results were all encouraging, but the mines' recovery will now be held back by the bullion price," one dealer said.
The gold index lost 40.5 points to 1,378 as gold was fixed in London at $350.10 an ounce, the lowest since September 15, 1993, before dropping to $349.90 on the spot market.
The biggest loser was Free State Consolidated Gold Mines Ltd, the world's largest gold producer, which dropped more than five percent to 32.50 rand a share.
Analysts said a recovery in bullion was unlikely in the short-term.

Duncan Ingram, mining analyst at Edey Rogers, said he saw no prospect of gold reviving this year, given uncertainty about European central banks' holdings of the metal in the run-up to Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
"So we are looking at a gold price of $350 for this year, improving next year to $360," he said.
Gold prices have been sliding since hitting a high of $417 an ounce last February, with investors around the world preferring to put their money into soaring stock markets.
With revenues under pressure, South Africa's gold mines will have to look to higher output and improved productivity to drive profit growth this year, analysts said.
But it will be an uphill struggle. Last year South African gold production fell below 500 tonnes for the first time in 40 years and the industry expects little improvement in 1997.
"Just write off golds. They are a relic from the past," said one despondent share dealer.
